calculator.title: Tire pressure, load, and cornering force demonstration
calculator.description: Use a generic rubber baseline to show how rider, bike, pressure, tire width, speed, and lean change contact area and force; the model does not return a production pressure recommendation.

dashboard.provenanceLabel: Load source: {load}; tire-width source: {width}; tire-body calculation baseline: {body}
dashboard.fixedPressureHint: Fixed pressure enters A = Fz ÷ P for the load-bearing area estimate. The grip baseline is Fgrip = μ × Fz × Cbody, with Cbody fixed at 1. In the current Coulomb friction baseline, μ is independent of pressure. A pressure-sensitive μ requires sourced test data.
dashboard.title: Tire pressure, load, and cornering force demonstration
dashboard.subtitle: Pressure · load · speed · lean · contact area and dynamic force data
dashboard.noticeBody: This dashboard visualizes a provisional physics model. It does not issue a production tire-pressure recommendation. Follow tire, rim, and wheel manufacturer limits.
dashboard.controlBaselineBody: This dashboard uses a simplified first-order baseline to demonstrate how pressure, load, speed, tire width, and lean angle change force and contact area. The road is fixed to one flat-road condition. The result is an explanatory calculation only, not a measured tire test or a production safety limit.
dashboard.scienceTitle: 3. Physics notes: load, pressure, and force
dashboard.mechanicalBody: The generic tire-body condition is fixed at normalized baseline 1 in this calculation; contact area shows the relationship between load and pressure. The result is a calculation display, not a measured tire test.
dashboard.riskBody: Changing pressure changes the estimated contact area. The model does not simulate tread or compound changes.
dashboard.scopeBody: The current production API returns loads and supplied limits only. No uncalibrated pressure recommendation is presented.
dashboard.speedHint: At a fixed lean, speed changes the equivalent turn radius: R = v² / (g·tanθ).
dashboard.fixedMuHint: One fixed coefficient is used to demonstrate force relationships; it is not a road or tire measurement.
dashboard.diagnosticBody: At {speed} km/h and {lean}° lean, the equivalent turn radius is about {radius} m; front/rear lateral demand is {front} / {rear} N. The data panel shows the backend's force and contact-area estimates.

intro.matching: For safety and performance, match the exact tire, rim, and wheelset using each manufacturer's documents, especially for tubeless and hookless systems. This page does not infer compatibility from a brand, model year, or technology label; without an article-level source, the result remains unknown.
intro.width: Inner rim width changes the mounted tire shape and measured width. Width and pressure must be evaluated with the exact tire, rim, and wheel documents; an uncalibrated width coefficient is not a safety limit.
intro.etrto: Hookless pressure and tire restrictions depend on the exact rim, wheel, and tire instructions. Check each document and follow the lowest applicable limit. Do not assume a universal ceiling from rim type alone or mark a model compatible when its source is missing.

why.title: 1. Why tire pressure matters
why.performance: Too high means less grip; too low means more rolling resistance.
why.safety: Overinflation can damage rims; underinflation increases the risk of pinch flats.
why.comfort: Correct pressure reduces vibration and improves ride quality.

riderWeight.adjustment: Adjust only within the exact tire, rim, and wheel manufacturer ranges; do not apply a generic psi increment.

tireWidth.explanation: Wider tires can run lower pressure.
tireWidth.adjustment: Width affects mounted shape and load distribution, but it does not produce a pressure value by itself. Use the exact model's manufacturer range.

terrain.explanation: Soft or muddy terrain needs lower pressure for grip; rocky terrain needs higher pressure for rim protection.

ridingStyle.explanation: Aggressive racing needs higher pressure; casual riding can use lower pressure.
ridingStyle.adjustment: Riding style can guide a choice within the exact manufacturer range; it does not create a universal pressure number.

rimDesign.explanation: Wider rims support lower pressure; narrow rims require higher pressure.

typical.title: 3. Typical pressure ranges (approximate)
typical.road: Road pressure examples must come from the exact tire, rim, and wheel documents; different models cannot share one range.
typical.mountain: Mountain pressure depends on the exact tire model, rim inner width, load, terrain, and the manufacturer's limits.
typical.city: City and commuter setups also require the pressure range printed for the exact tire and rim.

tips.title: 4. Practical tips
tips.sidewall: Check the sidewall and follow the manufacturer's recommended range.
tips.gauge: Use a reliable gauge instead of relying on feel.
tips.inspect: Inspect regularly because tires lose air naturally; check weekly or before rides.
tips.extremes: Avoid extremes: never exceed the maximum or drop below the minimum pressure.
tips.seasonal: Adjust only within the range supplied for the exact tire, rim, and wheel setup.

warnings.title: 5. Risks & warnings
warnings.high: Too high: harsh ride and potential rim damage.
warnings.low: Too low: pinch flats and poor handling.
warnings.neglect: Neglecting checks: gradual air loss reduces performance and safety.
warnings.hookless: Hookless systems have no universal ceiling supplied by this page; follow the lowest applicable limit in the exact tire, rim, and wheel documents.
